column6: Hannah warns the proud against arrogant speech because God weighs actions; the commentary likewise locates distinction in deeds rather than the rank people claim.
Hannah says the Lord makes poor and rich, lowers and raises; noble or low standing is unstable before divine choice.
Hannah says God lifts the poor from dust to sit with princes; the lowest people can receive the highest place.
The psalm says God raises the poor from dust; it reverses the commentary's social description of the lowest people.
God seats the needy with the princes of his people; inherited social distance is overturned.
A foreigner joined to the Lord is told not to say that God will separate him from the people; belonging is opened beyond ancestry.
The Lord addresses eunuchs who choose what pleases him and keep his covenant; a person without descendants can gain divine standing through conduct.

column5: name better than sons and daughters
column6: God promises faithful eunuchs a lasting name better than sons and daughters; this directly reverses the loss of lineage as a measure of worth.
Foreigners who join the Lord, serve him, and keep covenant are included; loyalty and action outrank birth.
God accuses powerful sheep of pushing the weak with flank, shoulder, and horns; this adds the mechanism by which rank harms the weak and lost in the commentary.

column5: خ س ر / Hebrew חסר; table sound correspondence only
column6: The righteous eats to satisfaction while the wicked person's stomach lacks, using חסר; deficiency is distributed by moral standing, not inherited rank.

column5: ء ن س / Hebrew אנש; table BDB Arabic cognate
column6: Job's friend asks whether mortal enosh can be righteous before God; the cognate human category is placed under a universal moral question.

column5: learned outcast precedes ignorant high priest
column6: The Mishnah's status ladder gives way when a learned person of stigmatized birth outranks an ignorant high priest; acquired fidelity to teaching displaces pedigree.

column5: honor measured by fear of God
column6: Sirach asks which human stock deserves honor and answers in terms of fearing the Lord rather than ancestry; it gives the commentary's rank reversal an explicit criterion.
Wisdom says powerful rulers face strict examination while the lowly may receive mercy; high rank increases accountability instead of securing safety.

column5: rulers use their unbelief as test
column6: The authorities ask whether any ruler or Pharisee has believed in Jesus; they make elite standing a test of truth, like the elite objection to Noah's lowly followers.

column5: crowd dismissed as ignorant and cursed
column6: The authorities call the believing crowd ignorant of the law and cursed; this closely matches discrediting a message by degrading its low status adherents.
Scribes ask why Jesus eats with tax collectors and sinners; the objection attacks a teacher through the people who follow and gather around him.
Pharisees and scribes grumble that Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them; association with despised people becomes their reason to reject him.
Council members see Peter and John as uneducated ordinary men yet recognize their boldness and connection with Jesus; low standing does not discredit their witness.

column5: healed man dismissed as unfit to teach
column6: The authorities tell the formerly blind man he was born entirely in sin and expel him when he challenges them; presumed low status overrides the truth of his testimony.
Jesus says tax collectors and prostitutes enter God's kingdom ahead of his religious interlocutors; socially disgraced people outrank the prestigious by response to God.
James tells the lowly brother to boast in exaltation; faith gives a rank opposite to his social place.
James tells the rich person to boast in humiliation because wealth fades; high worldly rank cannot protect a person from loss.
Paul names Greek, Jew, barbarian, Scythian, slave, and free, then makes Christ central to all; despised ethnic and servile labels cannot set rank in this community.

column5: master and slave share impartial judge
column6: Masters are told to abandon threats because their Master in heaven shows no favoritism; the hierarchy over dependent people is judged by one standard.

column5: rich commanded to be rich in works
column6: The wealthy are instructed to do good and be rich in good works; ethical action replaces possessions as the relevant kind of wealth.
Jesus tells those claiming Abraham as father that true children would do Abraham's deeds; a claimed ancestor must be matched by conduct.
John demands fruit fitting repentance immediately before challenging reliance on Abrahamic descent; conduct supplies the missing criterion for the lineage claim.

column5: all have sinned and fall short
column6: Paul says all have sinned and fall short of God's glory; the universal human condition resembles the commentary's loss of insan before its exception.
Paul immediately says people are justified freely through Christ; this supplies the saving answer to the preceding universal shortfall.

column5: all die in Adam, made alive in Christ
column6: Paul places death on all through Adam and life in Christ; one human lineage shares loss while a new relation changes the outcome.
James calls faith dead when it lacks works; the surah commentary expressly says its exception requires both belief and action.
Believers are described as created in Christ for good works; the commentary's exception likewise joins faith to enacted righteousness.

column5: one fate for righteous and wicked
column6: Qoheleth says the righteous and wicked share the same fate of death; its earthly leveling sharpens the commentary's claim that faith and deeds distinguish people from loss.
Qoheleth says no righteous person on earth does good without sin; it intensifies the commentary's universal statement about humanity before the exception.
Ezekiel says a wicked person who turns from sin and keeps God's statutes shall live; action can change the fate inherited status cannot.
Ezekiel says former righteousness cannot save someone who turns to injustice; even a favorable standing cannot replace continuing conduct.
The psalm orders rescue of the weak and needy from wicked hands; it treats the lowly as people to defend, rather than as a contemptible class.

column5: giving to poor as lending to God
column6: Kindness to the poor is treated as a loan to the Lord who repays; conduct toward lowly people carries divine weight.

column5: ء ن س / Hebrew אנש; table BDB Arabic cognate
column6: The human heart is described as deeply sick, using a form of אנש; the same listed root's weakness sense gives a moral dimension to human vulnerability, though its relation to Arabic insan is uncertain.

column5: ء ن س / Hebrew אנש; table BDB Arabic cognate
column6: Bildad calls enosh a maggot before God; his harsh image lowers every mortal irrespective of ancestry or social position.
The rabbinic account has Noah's contemporaries challenge his ark building and warning; it adds ridicule to the Noah scene, although it does not say they object to his followers' rank.
Jesus asks what it profits someone to gain the whole world and forfeit life; worldly gain can become the personal loss named in the commentary.

column5: rich told not to be haughty
column6: The rich are told not to set hope on uncertain riches but on God; high material standing offers no sure standing before him.

column5: once no people, now God's people
column6: The letter says its recipients once lacked peoplehood but now are God's people; belonging is conferred beyond inherited status.
Jesus forbids status titles among disciples because they have one teacher and are all siblings; kinship in faith levels rank.

column5: redeemed from every people and tribe
column6: A countless multitude from all nations and tribes stands before the throne; final belonging extends across lineages rather than following one noble stock.
